paragraphs: The paper studies adversarial attacks made without any access to the target classifier, including the ability to query it. In this setting, an attacker needs examples that transfer to a model it cannot inspect. Earlier approaches largely relied on empirical observations about what improves transfer, leaving a gap in theoretical justification.

Adversarial Example Games addresses this gap by treating attack generation as a competition between an attack generator and a classifier drawn from a specified hypothesis class, such as an architecture family. The generator and classifier are trained adversarially. The authors prove that the game has an equilibrium and that an optimal generator can produce attacks against any classifier within the corresponding class.

The guarantee concerns the optimal generator and its specified hypothesis class. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 also support the approach empirically: the authors report average relative improvements of 29.9% against undefended models and 47.2% against robust models over prior leading methods. Together, the theory and experiments connect transferable attack design to an explicit game formulation.
neurips-2020-adversarial-example-games-8.tldr: Adversarial Example Games gives a game-theoretic foundation for attacks that transfer across a specified classifier class without querying the target.

paragraphs: Deep clustering learns a representation of data and a way to divide that representation into groups together. The paper examines a vulnerability in this arrangement: small changes within the learned representation can cause substantially different cluster assignments. Without labels to anchor those assignments, the clustering component can be susceptible to adversarial manipulation.

The authors define adversarial examples directly in the embedding space, where the network represents its inputs. They then devise an attack that seeks examples capable of misleading the clustering layers while preserving the performance of the embedding component. This separates disruption of the grouping decision from damage to the representation itself and provides a focused way to investigate clustering robustness.

The paper also introduces a defense based on adversarial learning. On two datasets, the reported experiments show substantial improvements in robustness alongside better overall clustering performance. The method can be applied to multiple existing clustering frameworks, making its contribution broader than a single clustering architecture. These findings support adversarial training as a practical way to strengthen the grouping stage of deep clustering.
neurips-2020-adversarial-learning-for-ro.tldr: The paper develops embedding-space attacks and an adversarial defense that improve the robustness and performance of multiple deep clustering frameworks.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decision-making when feedback reveals only limited information about the consequences of an action. Finite stochastic partial monitoring provides a general framework for this situation. Although Thompson sampling had worked well in several online decision problems, its behavior in this framework lacked a theoretical analysis, and an existing implementation used a heuristic approximation to the posterior distribution.

The authors introduce a Thompson-sampling-based algorithm that can draw the target parameter exactly from its posterior. This addresses the sampling approximation directly. They also analyze a linearized version of the problem under local observability, a condition on how the available feedback supports distinguishing relevant decisions.

Under those conditions, the algorithm achieves problem-dependent expected pseudo-regret growing only logarithmically with the number of rounds. This means its expected cumulative decision disadvantage has a slowly growing bound, with constants that depend on the problem. The result supplies the first Thompson sampling regret bound for partial monitoring and also the first logarithmic bound for linear bandits. The stated guarantee is tied to the analyzed variant and observability condition.
neurips-2020-analysis-and-design-of-thom.tldr: A new Thompson sampling algorithm enables exact posterior sampling and achieves logarithmic expected pseudo-regret for a locally observable, linearized partial-monitoring problem.

paragraphs: The paper considers controlling a system whose state evolves according to known linear dynamics. The system experiences stochastic noise, while costs can be selected adversarially. After acting, the controller observes only the cost it actually incurred. It does not receive the whole cost function, so it cannot directly evaluate what other decisions would have cost.

The authors develop an efficient control algorithm for this restricted-feedback setting. When costs are strongly convex and smooth, they prove that regret grows with the square root of the number of time steps. This sublinear growth means the regret per step decreases as the interaction continues, despite the limited feedback and adversarial choice of costs.

A central technical ingredient handles bandit optimization when losses depend on past decisions. That memory matters in control because an action changes the system state and can influence later costs. The paper also extends its results to general convex costs that may be nonsmooth and to non-stochastic system noise. These extensions broaden the setting beyond the assumptions supporting the main square-root regret result.
neurips-2020-bandit-linear-control-227b6.tldr: An efficient algorithm controls known linear systems using only incurred-cost feedback, achieving square-root regret for strongly convex, smooth costs.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization concerns making a sequence of decisions as loss information becomes available. Regret measures the cumulative disadvantage of those decisions against a comparison choice. This paper develops algorithms with improved full-matrix regret bounds, addressing how an online learner can adapt its updates while retaining theoretical guarantees.

One contribution is to incorporate constraints without requiring learning rates tuned using unavailable oracle information. Another revisits full-matrix AdaGrad: the authors identify a learning rate that gives a better regret guarantee and show how to adjust toward it during learning. The practical significance of this theoretical design is that the favorable rate need not be supplied in advance using unknown information.

The results come from a general framework for constructing regret bounds that depend on an arbitrary sequence of norms. Norms specify how the analysis measures the sizes of updates or other quantities, so allowing a sequence gives the framework flexibility as learning proceeds. The contribution combines stronger guarantees, automatic learning-rate adjustment, and support for constrained decisions within a common analytical approach.
neurips-2020-better-full-matrix-regret-v.tldr: The paper improves full-matrix online-learning regret guarantees while adapting learning rates automatically and supporting constraints.

paragraphs: The paper studies how multiplicative weights updates and its optimistic variant evolve when used to learn in games. Instead of tracking action probabilities directly, the authors analyze accumulated action payoffs. They follow the volume occupied by a collection of initial conditions as the learning rule moves those conditions forward, revealing properties of whole groups of trajectories.

For zero-sum games, ordinary multiplicative weights expands volume and exhibits Lyapunov chaos, while its optimistic variant contracts volume. The contraction gives another perspective on the optimistic method's known convergence. However, the relationship reverses in coordination games. The effect of optimism therefore depends on the interaction between the learning algorithm and the type of game.

The volume analysis also establishes two negative properties of ordinary multiplicative weights in zero-sum games. Even with a unique equilibrium assigning positive probability to every action, trajectories repeatedly linger near pure-strategy profiles that are unstable from a game-theoretic perspective. In addition, under the paper's broad interpretation of good states, the dynamics cannot avoid bad states forever. These results expose behavior that equilibrium existence alone does not describe.
neurips-2020-chaos-extremism-and-optimis.tldr: Tracking evolving volumes reveals chaos and recurring extreme behavior in multiplicative weights, while showing that optimism's effects depend on the game.

paragraphs: COT-GAN is an adversarial method for training generative models to produce sequences. Its central design choice is to compare generated and real data using causal optimal transport. This extends ordinary optimal transport with a temporal causality constraint, bringing the order and information structure of a sequence into the training objective.

The causality condition also helps define what the discriminator learns. The authors use it to parameterize a cost that acts as a robust, worst-case distance between distributions. This gives the adversarial comparison a framework suited to time-dependent data. An entropy penalty makes the transport calculation compatible with the Sinkhorn algorithm, providing a computational route for evaluating the loss during training.

The paper additionally introduces an improved Sinkhorn divergence that shows less bias in learning. The authors identify this improvement as part of the method's success. Experiments demonstrate effective and stable generation of both low-dimensional and high-dimensional time series. The findings support combining a temporal constraint, a learned transport cost, and an adjusted divergence when building generative models for sequential data.
neurips-2020-cot-gan-generating-sequenti.tldr: COT-GAN combines causal optimal transport with an improved Sinkhorn divergence to train effective, stable generators of time-series data.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to minimize a strongly convex function when only noisy measurements of its values are available. The learner must choose evaluation points sequentially without observing derivatives. The authors investigate how higher-order smoothness changes both the final optimization error and the regret accumulated while searching.

Their algorithm approximates projected gradient descent using a randomized gradient estimate. Each estimate combines two function evaluations with a smoothing kernel. This turns value measurements into information suitable for a gradient-style update. The analysis covers both constrained problems, where the search must remain within an allowed set, and unconstrained problems.

The authors prove upper bounds for their algorithm and minimax lower bounds that apply to any sequential search method in the studied setting. Comparing the two establishes near-optimal dependence on sample complexity and problem parameters. They also use the algorithm to estimate the minimum function value, obtaining nearly sharp oracle behavior. The work therefore addresses both locating a good solution and estimating how low the objective can go, while quantifying the value of additional smoothness.
neurips-2020-exploiting-higher-order-smo.tldr: A two-evaluation randomized gradient method exploits higher-order smoothness to achieve nearly optimal noisy derivative-free optimization guarantees.

paragraphs: Deep generative models can assign higher likelihood to unfamiliar outliers than to examples from the distribution they were trained to represent. This paper investigates a possible explanation for that counterintuitive behavior. Its starting point is that the region with the highest probability density need not coincide with the model's typical set.

That distinction changes how likelihood should be interpreted for outlier detection. A point receiving a high density value is not automatically representative of the distribution's typical behavior. Building on this perspective, the authors propose a new outlier test. Its empirical success suggests that a failed likelihood-based detection rule does not, by itself, establish that the generative model is uncalibrated.

Additional experiments examine the roles of low-level texture and high-level semantic content in distinguishing outliers. This asks what kinds of differences a detection benchmark actually rewards a model for noticing. Taken together, the results suggest that standard evaluations and benchmarks need modification. The paper offers an explanatory account and supporting experiments, while retaining the distinction between a detector's failure and the quality of the underlying generative model.
neurips-2020-further-analysis-of-outlier.tldr: The paper proposes typicality as a possible explanation for high-likelihood outliers and develops an empirically successful alternative detection test.

paragraphs: Bayesian models with latent Gaussian variables can produce posterior distributions whose geometry makes sampling difficult and slow. The paper studies a strategy that first uses a Laplace approximation to marginalize those latent variables. Dynamic Hamiltonian Monte Carlo then handles the remaining hyperparameters, reducing the part of the model that must be sampled directly.

The computational challenge is obtaining gradients of the approximate marginal likelihood efficiently. The authors derive an adjoint differentiation method that passes along only the information needed to construct those gradients. For high-dimensional hyperparameters, this method is reported to be orders of magnitude faster than existing leading differentiation techniques.

The approach is prototyped in Stan and tested on several models, including one with roughly 6,000 hyperparameters. Depending on the model, the embedded Laplace approximation can ease problematic posterior geometry and produce a dramatic speed-up. The contribution combines an approximation to latent-variable integration with a more scalable way to differentiate that approximation. Its benefits are case-dependent, and the resulting marginal likelihood remains an approximation.
neurips-2020-hamiltonian-monte-carlo-usi.tldr: An efficient adjoint method accelerates gradients for Laplace-approximated Bayesian inference, enabling substantial speed-ups in some latent Gaussian models.

paragraphs: Compressing a large vector or matrix clearly reduces storage, but it does not automatically make computations equally cheap. This paper asks whether basic linear algebra can operate at a cost determined by the compressed size. It studies lossless representations and operations including inner products, matrix-vector products, and matrix multiplication.

The answer depends on the compression scheme. For run-length encoding, an inner product can be computed in time linear in the compressed representation's size. The authors show that richer grammar-based compression behaves differently. Under complexity assumptions, worst-case computations can require essentially quadratic or even larger runtimes in the compressed size, ruling out the hoped-for linear-time behavior.

The grammar-compression class includes popular methods such as the Lempel-Ziv family, which can compress more effectively than run-length encoding. The results therefore identify a tradeoff between obtaining a compact representation and making that representation convenient for computation. They do not say that every compressed input is hard; the lower bounds concern worst-case instances under stated complexity assumptions. Stronger compression alone cannot guarantee proportionally faster linear algebra.
neurips-2020-impossibility-results-for-g.tldr: Under complexity assumptions, grammar-based compression cannot generally make basic linear algebra run as cheaply as its compressed size might suggest.

paragraphs: The paper asks how the number of episodes needed to learn a near-optimal policy changes as planning horizons grow. It studies tabular, episodic reinforcement learning with cumulative rewards normalized to the unit interval. This normalization keeps the accuracy target comparable across horizons, rather than letting longer episodes automatically increase the scale of the value being estimated.

The authors prove that the required episode count can depend only logarithmically on the horizon. This refutes a conjecture that a polynomial dependence was unavoidable. The conclusion concerns normalized values and minimax sample complexity measured in episodes; it does not equate an episode's length with its count.

Two ideas support the result. First, the authors construct a covering collection of near-optimal policies whose logarithmic size grows only logarithmically with the horizon. Second, Online Trajectory Synthesis adaptively evaluates a supplied policy class using a number of episodes that scales logarithmically with the class's size. Together, these ideas show that long planning horizons need not impose the previously conjectured growth in episode requirements under the paper's formulation.
neurips-2020-is-long-horizon-rl-more-dif.tldr: For tabular episodic reinforcement learning with normalized rewards, near-optimal learning can require only logarithmic dependence on horizon in the number of episodes.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization trains against unfavorable distributions within a specified uncertainty set. This paper develops algorithms for convex losses using conditional value at risk, or CVaR, and chi-squared divergence uncertainty sets. Its focus is making these robust objectives practical at large scale without repeatedly processing the entire training set.

The authors prove bounds on the number of gradient evaluations that are independent of training-set size and parameter count. For chi-squared uncertainty sets, they provide the first such guarantees. For CVaR, the bound grows linearly with the uncertainty level, improving on earlier quadratic dependence. Lower bounds establish worst-case optimality for CVaR and a penalized version of the chi-squared problem.

The technical analysis controls the bias of estimating robust risk from batches and the variance of a multilevel Monte Carlo gradient estimator. These controls explain how smaller computations can still support rigorous optimization guarantees. Experiments on MNIST and ImageNet confirm the predicted scaling and report efficiency improvements of 9–36 times over full-batch methods. The dimension-independent statement concerns gradient-evaluation counts, rather than the cost of every individual evaluation.
neurips-2020-large-scale-methods-for-dis.tldr: The paper gives scalable algorithms for convex distributionally robust optimization with gradient-evaluation guarantees independent of dataset size and parameter count.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated games in which a learner acts first and an opponent responds to that action. The learner does not know the opponent's response model in advance. This makes choosing a rewarding action inseparable from learning how the opponent reacts, especially when the learner faces an adversarial sequence of opponents.

The authors impose kernel-based regularity assumptions to describe exploitable structure in those responses. Their algorithm combines bilevel optimization, which accounts for the responding player's decision, with online learning. It balances exploration of the unknown response model against exploitation of actions that currently appear rewarding.

The resulting regret guarantees grow sublinearly with the number of rounds and depend on the regularity of the opponents' responses. Thus, the theoretical promise comes from learning structured responses, rather than assuming arbitrary unknown behavior is equally manageable. The authors also specialize the method to repeated Stackelberg games and demonstrate it in traffic routing and wildlife conservation tasks. These examples support the usefulness of jointly learning an opponent's behavior and deciding how to act before that opponent responds.
neurips-2020-learning-to-play-sequential.tldr: A kernel-based online algorithm learns unknown opponents' responses while achieving sublinear regret under response-regularity assumptions.

paragraphs: Matrix completion estimates missing entries using the entries already observed. This paper supplements those observations with graphs describing social relationships or item similarity. Its central idea is to exploit a graph's hierarchy, including relationships between groups, rather than using only a flat division into separate communities.

The authors propose a parameter-free, computationally efficient algorithm that begins with hierarchical graph clustering. It then repeatedly improves both the graph clustering and the estimated matrix ratings. This alternating refinement allows the two sources of information to support one another as the estimates develop.

Under a hierarchical stochastic block model for the graph and a specified low-rank rating model, the algorithm reaches the information-theoretic limit on the required number of observed entries. The authors establish that limit through maximum-likelihood analysis and an impossibility lower bound. Their result shows that using relationships across groups can substantially reduce sample requirements compared with identifying groups alone. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the theory and report significant gains over other graph-assisted matrix completion methods.
neurips-2020-matrix-completion-with-hier.tldr: An iterative matrix-completion algorithm exploits hierarchical graph relationships to achieve optimal sample complexity under the paper's graph and rating models.

paragraphs: A network can be large enough to represent a good predictor without being easy for a training algorithm to find. Many earlier theoretical learning guarantees bridged that gap by requiring networks much larger than representation alone demanded. This paper investigates whether stochastic gradient descent can succeed with network sizes closer to what the task intrinsically requires.

The authors prove guarantees for depth-two neural networks on several tasks: memorizing samples, learning polynomials with bounded weights, and learning certain kernel spaces. Across these settings, they obtain near-optimal network size, sample complexity, and runtime. The contribution concerns the resources needed by a concrete learning algorithm, rather than only the existence of suitable network parameters.

A specific memorization result uses roughly m divided by d hidden neurons to fit m randomly labeled points on the sphere in d dimensions, up to logarithmic factors. The total parameter count is roughly m, again up to logarithmic factors. This shows that successful optimization need not require the very large excess parameter counts used in many prior guarantees for the tasks studied.
neurips-2020-neural-networks-learning-an.tldr: The paper proves that stochastic gradient descent can memorize and learn specified function classes with depth-two networks using nearly optimal resources.

paragraphs: The paper studies bandit problems with so many possible actions that their number is comparable to, or much larger than, the number of available rounds. Multiple actions may be optimal or nearly optimal. The learner is not given structural information about the actions and does not know how many best actions exist, which determines the problem's hardness.

The authors first develop an algorithm that adapts without knowing this hardness level and prove a regret bound. They also establish an impossibility result: no algorithm can be minimax optimal at every hardness level simultaneously in this setting. Their algorithm achieves a Pareto-optimal rate function, expressing an optimal tradeoff across those levels rather than uniform optimality everywhere.

The situation improves when the expected reward of a best action is supplied as additional information. With that knowledge, a second adaptive algorithm is minimax optimal across all hardness levels up to polylogarithmic factors. Experiments support the theoretical guarantees and show advantages over prior leading methods. The results identify both the value and the limits of adapting to an unknown abundance of good actions.
neurips-2020-on-regret-with-multiple-bes.tldr: Adaptive bandit algorithms exploit multiple good actions, with provable tradeoffs that improve when the best action's expected reward is known.

paragraphs: Parameter Ensembling by Perturbation creates an ensemble by adding Gaussian noise to a trained network's parameters. A single variance controls the perturbation size. The method chooses that variance by maximizing the validation log-likelihood of the ensemble's averaged predictions, starting from zero variance, which recovers the original model.

Empirically, the authors find a well-defined likelihood maximum as the variance increases. Calibration, or the agreement between predictive confidence and outcomes, also tends to improve up to that point. Most experiments show small predictive-performance gains, while some show substantial calibration gains. Tests with pretrained ImageNet networks report better likelihood and calibration together with mild classification-accuracy improvements.

The paper relates the likelihood gain to the mean curvature of the likelihood function and empirical Fisher information. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 also connect the effect to overfitting, supporting its use as a probe of training behavior. PEP requires no special architecture or training procedure, and pretrained networks need no additional training. Its empirical appeal is obtaining useful ensembles from perturbations around an already trained solution.
neurips-2020-pep-parameter-ensembling-by.tldr: PEP ensembles Gaussian perturbations of trained parameters, often improving likelihood and calibration without additional training of pretrained networks.

paragraphs: Structural equation models are used to investigate causal relationships and estimate structural quantities in complex systems. This paper studies a generalized class in which the quantity to estimate is defined by a linear operator equation. The problem is to turn that mathematical definition into a tractable neural-network estimation procedure with a convergence guarantee.

The authors express the equation as a min-max game and represent both players with neural networks. They learn the network parameters using stochastic gradient descent. Their analysis covers both two-layer and multilayer networks with ReLU activations, connecting an adversarial training formulation to the original estimation task.

The convergence proof uses online-learning techniques and local linear approximations of the networks. It establishes global convergence in an overparameterized regime where the number of neurons diverges. Within that regime, the paper provides a computationally tractable neural estimator with provable convergence and no requirement to split the sample. The significance is a theoretical bridge between neural adversarial optimization and structural estimation, with the convergence claim explicitly tied to the network-width regime.
neurips-2020-provably-efficient-neural-e.tldr: A neural min-max formulation yields structural-equation estimators with global convergence guarantees in a diverging-width regime, without sample splitting.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to learn policies that generalize compositionally: using learned components effectively when they appear in different combinations. Its approach begins with a teacher policy that already earns high reward. A second stage refactors that policy into a student whose architecture supplies a strong bias toward the desired kind of generalization.

The student is object-centered and uses a graph neural network. Its input objects are learned from images through self-supervised learning. This puts objects and their organization at the center of the student's decision process. The two-stage framework combines the teacher's successful behavior with a student representation designed to support composition.

The authors evaluate the approach on four difficult tasks that require compositional generalization and report better performance than the comparison methods. These empirical findings support transferring a successful policy into an architecture structured around objects. The contribution brings together policy refactoring, self-supervised object discovery, and graph-based decision-making as a way to improve generalization beyond the combinations encountered during learning.
neurips-2020-refactoring-policy-for-comp.tldr: A two-stage framework refactors a high-reward teacher into an object-centered graph-network student that improves compositional generalization on four tasks.

paragraphs: Residual shortcuts help train very deep networks, but they also require earlier feature maps to remain in memory until later computations finish. The paper reports that shortcuts account for about 40% of feature-map memory usage during ResNet-50 inference. It therefore asks whether training can benefit from a residual network while deployment uses a plain network without shortcuts.

The proposed joint-training framework sends early feature maps from the plain network through later stages of both the plain and residual networks. Losses from these paths produce a mixture of gradients used to update the plain network. This gives the plain model training support from its residual counterpart and addresses vanishing gradients.

Experiments on ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 report accuracy at the same level as the ResNet baseline, with about 1.4 times faster execution and a 1.25-fold memory reduction. Fine-tuning ImageNet-pretrained plain networks on MIT 67 and Caltech 101 also yields slightly higher performance than the ResNet-50 baseline. The results support retaining the training benefits of residual connections while deploying a more economical architecture.
neurips-2020-residual-distillation-towar.tldr: Joint training transfers residual-network gradient support to plain CNNs that achieve comparable accuracy with faster, lower-memory inference.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how much Safe and Seldonian reinforcement-learning methods depend on accurate training data. Its focus is the effect of corrupted data on algorithms intended to support safe decision-making. This connects the reliability of a learned policy to the integrity of the information used to train it.

The authors introduce a security measure based on an attacker model representing worst-case perturbations of the training data. They use that measure to examine susceptibility to corruption and find that a couple of Seldonian methods are extremely sensitive even when only a few data points are corrupted. This is a targeted finding about the studied methods, rather than a statement that every safe-learning algorithm behaves identically.

The paper then proposes an algorithm with greater robustness to data corruption. Demonstrations include a grid-world problem and a diabetes treatment simulation. These applications illustrate how the method can be used within reinforcement-learning problems while keeping the evidence at the level of the studied settings. The contribution combines an explicit way to assess training-data security with an algorithm designed to improve it.
neurips-2020-security-analysis-of-safe-a.tldr: A worst-case security analysis exposes corruption sensitivity in selected Seldonian RL methods and motivates a more robust algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper develops an asymptotically precise analysis of linear classifiers with multiple classes. It asks how test error changes with the training algorithm, data distribution, problem dimensions, and number of classes. The analysis also accounts for class frequencies and correlations within and between classes, making it possible to examine several sources of classification difficulty together.

A major obstacle is that multiclass test error depends on complicated properties of the trained model, including correlations between learned weight vectors. This difficulty appears even when training minimizes a simple squared loss. The authors introduce theoretical techniques that overcome some of these obstacles and characterize the relevant asymptotic behavior.

The analysis shows that classification performance depends strongly on the data distribution. Different algorithms can be optimal for different distributions or different amounts of training data and features. Thus, conclusions about which method performs best depend on the statistical setting being analyzed. The work provides precise results for the studied linear classifiers and suggests a possible foundation for analyzing additional classification algorithms.
neurips-2020-theoretical-insights-into-m.tldr: An asymptotically precise theory of linear multiclass classification shows how test error and the best-performing algorithm depend on the data and problem dimensions.

paragraphs: Learning theory often uses combinatorial dimensions to describe which problems can be learned under particular rules. This paper seeks an analogous characterization when a learner has limited memory. The setting is realizable strong learning under a known distribution, so the proposed characterization addresses a specific statistical and computational framework.

The authors construct a candidate measure using the statistical-query dimension of neighboring distributions. They prove upper and lower bounds based on this candidate, connecting sufficient resources for learning with resources that are unavoidable. In some parameter regimes, the bounds match, yielding a characterization of strong learning under memory constraints.

Within the regime where the bounds coincide, bounded-memory learning and statistical-query learning are equivalent. This connects two ways of restricting a learner: limiting its storage and restricting how it obtains statistical information. The authors identify this as the first characterization of strong learning under space constraints in any regime. They conjecture that the result extends to a substantially wider range of parameters, but that broader claim remains a conjecture.
neurips-2020-towards-a-combinatorial-cha.tldr: A statistical-query-based combinatorial measure characterizes bounded-memory strong learning in a particular parameter regime, with a broader characterization conjectured.

paragraphs: The paper asks what computations spiking neural networks perform. Previous work had connected time-averaged firing rates in several networks to solutions of convex optimization problems. The authors broaden this perspective, showing how virtually all inhibition-dominated spiking networks can be understood through convex optimization, with their connectivity, timescales, and firing thresholds linked to optimization parameters.

This viewpoint gives a geometric account of the networks' behavior. For a particular class of networks, the authors establish that instantaneous output solves linear or quadratic programming problems. That result makes the mapping from input to output explicit, going beyond an account based only on firing rates averaged over time.

Using these connections, the authors derive local supervised learning rules that can approximate specified convex input-output functions. The resulting networks are consistent with several biological features, including low and irregular firing, balance between excitation and inhibition, and robustness to perturbations and synaptic delays. The work links a network's physical and dynamical properties to a mathematical computation, then uses that link to guide learning.
neurips-2020-understanding-spiking-netwo.tldr: Convex optimization explains a broad class of inhibition-dominated spiking networks and yields local learning rules for approximating convex input-output functions.
